extracted.intended_audience: researchers of peer review and bibliometrics; journal editors and policy-makers interested in manuscript selection utility
extracted.subtask_short: evaluating peer review utility for journals
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing how useful peer review ratings are for editors' manuscript selection decisions using utility analysis (Taylor–Russell model), bibliometric proxies (citation counts, R_w), and observed editorial decision rules in a high-impact chemistry journal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validity coefficient (predictive validity, r_xy)
rubrics_metrics.description: The strength of the relationship between the predictor (outcome of peer review, reviewers' ratings) and the criterion (scientific quality of a submission, measured ex post).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher r_xy (greater correlation) narrows the bivariate point cloud ellipse and increases the probability that qualified submissions are accepted. Validity can be estimated (here by Spearman's rank-order correlation). Note that more reviewers per manuscript do not necessarily increase observed validity if editors' behavior (e.g., waiting for more reviews only when decision is unclear) affects which manuscripts get additional reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base rate
rubrics_metrics.description: The percentage of submissions that are 'qualified' (fundamentally suitable for publication; after publication they are comparatively frequently cited).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A high base rate reduces the added utility of peer review for selection. Editors/journals can aim to increase base rate via submission policy and pre-selection to encourage self-selection by authors (clear description of journal scope/standards).

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection rate
rubrics_metrics.description: The percentage of submissions that are accepted for publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lowering the selection rate can increase the success rate (percentage of accepted submissions that are qualified) but only if there is a positive validity coefficient (r_xy>0). Very low selection rates can also lead to many qualified manuscripts being rejected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Success rate (utility)
rubrics_metrics.description: The percentage of accepted submissions that are qualified submissions (AQ/(AQ+AN)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Can be calculated directly from observed counts or taken from Taylor–Russell tables given base rate, selection rate and validity coefficient. Used as the primary measure of the usefulness of peer review for selection decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taylor–Russell utility model
rubrics_metrics.description: A model relating validity coefficient, base rate, selection rate, and success rate to determine practical effectiveness/utility of a selection process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the model and its tables to estimate how changes in base rate, selection rate, or validity affect success rate. The Taylor–Russell tables assume bivariate normal, linear, homoscedastic relationships between predictor and criterion; apply with caution if assumptions are violated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type I and Type II editorial errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Type I error: editors accept a manuscript that is not actually of high scientific impact (false positive). Type II error: editors reject a manuscript that later proves to be high impact (false negative).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify editorial decisions into AQ (accepted & qualified), AN (accepted & non-qualified), RQ (rejected & qualified), RN (rejected & non-qualified) to compute error rates and overall correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of citation counts as proxy for research quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Citation counts (here measured in a fixed time window) are used as an operationalizable proxy for the scientific quality or impact of a manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations measure one aspect (international impact) and are widely used but controversial. The paper uses a fixed three-year citation window and Chemical Abstracts (CA) data. Be explicit about metric choice and acknowledge limitations (fashion waves, journal reputation changes, non-quality drivers of citations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative Subfield Citedness (R_w) and impact-class thresholds
rubrics_metrics.description: R_w relates a paper's citations to the mean citations of papers in the same CA subject area. Van Raan thresholds: R_w <0.5 far below; 0.5–0.8 below; 0.8–1.2 approximately same; 1.2–1.5 above; R_w >1.5 far above.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use R_w to classify whether a paper is qualified for a high-impact journal; the authors used R_w>1.5 as the criterion cutoff for AC-IE. Choose subject-area reference sets (CA sections) carefully and state cutoffs explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion cutoff definition (example: R_w > 1.5 for AC-IE)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define what counts as a 'qualified' submission based on the journal's aims; for AC-IE the study classified submissions with R_w>1.5 (far above-average citation impact) as qualified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cutoff choice should reflect the journal's goals (e.g., maintaining high JIF). Be explicit about the cutoff and the rationale; report sensitivity to alternative thresholds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer evaluation questions (AC-IE reviewer form)
rubrics_metrics.description: AC-IE reviewer form (year 2000) included: (1) 'How important do you consider the results?' (very important/important/less important/unimportant); (2) 'Do the data verify the hypothesis and conclusions?' (yes/no); (3) 'Is the length appropriate?' (yes/too short/too long); (4) 'Do you recommend acceptance of the Communication?' (yes without alterations / yes after minor / yes but only after major / no).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These explicit questions form the predictor used by editors; ensure reviewers understand the meaning of categories. In 2008 a fifth question was added. Collecting structured review responses enables numeric scoring and operational decision rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision rule ('clear-cut rule') for acceptance (AC-IE)
rubrics_metrics.description: AC-IE's practice: generally accept a manuscript only if two reviewers rate the results as 'important' or 'very important' and also recommend publication (do not answer 'no' to the acceptance question). If based on one review, both positive answers are required from that reviewer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decision rules should be explicit and consistently applied. The study maps these rules to numeric predictor cutoffs (predictor cutoff = 3 with one review; 6 with two reviews; 8.5 with three reviews) using the scoring scheme described below.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer scoring mapping and predictor construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Convert categorical reviewer responses to numeric scores: importance (very important=3, important=2, less important=1, unimportant=0); recommendation (yes without alterations=3, yes after minor=2, yes after major=1, no=0). The predictor value is the sum of scores across questions and across reviewers (e.g., one reviewer max =6; three reviewers max =18).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use summed reviewer scores as predictor on x-axis; select predictor cutoff corresponding to the journal's decision rule. Transformations (e.g., log) may be applied to criterion but not predictor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of fixed citation window and data source
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure citation counts for a fixed time window (here three years after publication) and use a comprehensive database (Chemical Abstracts) for chemistry-related publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fixed windows give equal time spans for articles published in different years. Choice of database and citation window affects measured impact; state choices and justify them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logarithmic transformation of citation data for normality
rubrics_metrics.description: Citation counts were logarithmized as log(x+1) to better approximate normal distribution for regression and plotting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transform bibliometric counts when needed to approach normality assumptions for parametric analyses (but check residuals and robustness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumptions and limits for applying Taylor–Russell tables
rubrics_metrics.description: Taylor–Russell tables are appropriate only if the assumptions of bivariate normality, linearity, and homoscedasticity between predictor and criterion are fulfilled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If assumptions are violated (as is often the case for bibliometric data), use table values with reservations and prefer direct computation from observed AQ/AN/RQ/RN counts where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-selection / access review to increase base rate
rubrics_metrics.description: A pre-screening stage (e.g., ACP access review) asks whether a manuscript meets principal evaluation criteria (scientific significance, scientific quality, presentation quality) and only forwards those rated at least 'good' for full review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-selection reduces the number of unsuitable submissions and increases the base rate of qualified manuscripts entering full peer review, saving reviewer/editor time and costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principal evaluation criteria for pre-screening (example: ACP)
rubrics_metrics.description: ACP's access review criteria: (1) scientific significance (substantial contribution, new concepts/methods/data), (2) scientific quality (valid approach, balanced discussion), (3) presentation quality (clear, concise, good figures/tables, appropriate English). Response categories: excellent, good, fair, poor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require a minimum rating (e.g., 'good' on all criteria) for a manuscript to proceed to full review. These concrete criteria guide both editorial triage and authors about expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improving validity via reviewer guidance and operationalization of 'high quality'
rubrics_metrics.description: Validity could be increased (e.g., to r_xy=0.55) if reviewers have precise information on what constitutes a high-quality manuscript (operationalized as 'most accessed', 'most cited', or 'Highlights').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide reviewers with explicit standards/examples of target quality and clarity about selection rate to improve predictive ratings. Use training or exemplars to align reviewer judgments with the journal's impact goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of additional usefulness of peer review (manuscript improvement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review not only selects manuscripts but also often results in improvement of the final publication (editorial/reviewer suggestions increase manuscript quality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This function of peer review (improvement) is valuable but hard to quantify with selection-utility models; consider separate evaluation metrics or qualitative assessment for review-driven improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement caveats: ex-post vs ex-ante and external influences on citations
rubrics_metrics.description: Using ex-post citation counts to judge ex-ante suitability has limitations: events between submission and citation measurement (journal rise, fashion waves) can affect citations independently of intrinsic manuscript quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge and discuss these limitations; consider complementary quality criteria (logical rigor, replicability) and sensitivity analyses to assess robustness of conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Taylor–Russell tables for scenario analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Tables can be used to examine how hypothetical changes in base rate, selection rate, or validity coefficient would alter the success rate (utility) of the selection process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tables for approximate policy simulation (e.g., estimate gain in utility from increasing validity to 0.55 or lowering selection rate). Remember applicability depends on assumptions; treat table estimates as rough approximations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editor behavior and review-count policy implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors often wait for more reviews when the decision is unclear; this behavior can bias observed validity coefficients by introducing a non-random process for which manuscripts receive additional reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing reviewer-count policies, consider how editor practices interact with reviewer sampling — simply increasing number of reviewers per manuscript may not increase predictive validity without addressing selection bias in which manuscripts receive more reviews.
